passages.title: The Lost Key
sentences: Ben and Ana got off the bus after school.
Ben looked in his bag for the house key.
The key was gone.
Ben frowned and looked in every pocket.
Ana went back to the bus stop.
She looked under the bench.
Then she held up a shiny key.
Ben grinned.
"Thank you!" he said.

passages.title: The Rover Ramp
sentences: Priya brought her rover to the robot fair at Harbor Middle School.
Her job was to drive it up a steep wooden ramp.
The rover rolled halfway up and then stopped.
Its battery was empty.
Priya groaned and put her hands on her head.
She had worked on the rover for three weeks.
She found a charger and plugged the rover in.
While she waited, she checked every wire.
Twenty minutes later, she tried again.
This time the rover climbed all the way to the top.
Priya smiled at Ms. Ortiz.
She had fixed it all by herself.

passages.title: The Milkmaid and Her Pail
sentences: A farm girl walked to market with a pail of milk on her head.
As she walked, she made plans.
"I will sell this milk and buy some eggs," she thought.
"The eggs will hatch into chickens."
"I will sell the chickens and buy a new blue dress."
She smiled and gave a happy little skip.
She pictured the dress and tossed her head with pride.
The pail tipped over.
All the milk spilled onto the dusty road.
The girl looked at the empty pail.
Her eggs, her chickens and her new dress were all gone.
Tears came to her eyes.

credit.title: The Milkmaid and Her Pail
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Maya's Comic
sentences: The library put up a comic show, and Maya's comic was on the wall.
It was about a rock that rolled all the way down Lantern Peaks.
On the first day of the show, Maya stood at the back of the room.
Her hands felt cold, and her stomach felt tight.
This was the first time strangers would see her drawings.
What if they thought her comic was boring?
A boy of about eight stopped in front of it.
He read every box, and then he laughed out loud at the last one.
"The rock does a flip into the creek!" he told his dad.
Then he turned around and saw Maya's name tag.
"Did you draw that?" he asked. "Can you sign my map of the show?"
Maya signed her name in big letters.
She smiled the whole way home.
That night, she drew three new comics.

passages.title: The Old Oak
sentences: For many years, a giant oak tree stood in the middle of Harbor Park.
Sam and his friends met under it after school.
Pixel liked to nap in its shade.
But the tree was very old, and its trunk was soft and weak inside.
Workers from the town said it had to come down.
On Monday, workers cut the tree down.
Sam stood by the fence and looked at the empty spot.
His eyes filled with tears.
He would miss the shade and the bumpy roots where he sat.
On Saturday, Grandma Rose came to the park with a small oak in a pot.
Sam, Priya and Leo dug a hole and planted it in the same spot.
Sam patted the soil flat.
"One day, this tree will be big too," he said, and he smiled.

passages.title: Ben's Game Song
sentences: In music class, each student had to make a short song on the school computer.
Ben and Ana had already built a racing game together, so Ben decided to make music for it.
His first song was slow and soft.
When Ana played the game with his song, she yawned, and her car drifted off the track.
Ben slumped down in his chair and stared at the screen.
Then he had an idea.
He made the beat twice as fast and added loud drums.
This time, Ana leaned forward and gripped the controller tightly.
"This music makes me want to go faster!" she said, and she won the race.
On Friday, the music teacher played Ben's song for the whole class.
Three students asked if they could play the game, too.
Ben grinned and saved his song in a folder called Best Work.

passages.title: Kite Day
sentences: On Saturday, Priya and Maya carried a big red kite up to the lookout on Lantern Peaks.
They had spent two evenings building it from thin sticks, paper and string.
But when they reached the top, the air was completely still.
The kite just dragged through the grass behind them.
Maya sat down on a rock and sighed.
Priya checked the weather forecast on her phone.
"It says the wind will get stronger in the afternoon," she said.
So they ate their lunch on the rock and watched the clouds.
At two o'clock, the tall grass began to bend, and Maya's hair blew across her face.
Priya let out the string, and the kite rose higher and higher over the trees.
Maya laughed and clapped her hands.
Later, a line of gray clouds moved in from the sea, and the wind turned cold.
The girls wound up the string and walked down before the first drops of rain.
Maya was not upset, because the kite had flown higher than they had hoped.

passages.title: The Lark and Her Young Ones
sentences: A mother lark built her nest on the ground in the middle of a farmer's wheat field.
Her chicks hatched in spring and grew strong while the green wheat grew tall around them.
By summer, the wheat had turned golden, and the young larks were almost ready to fly.
One morning, while their mother was away finding food, the farmer and his son walked into the field.
"This wheat is ripe," said the farmer. "We must ask our neighbors to come and help us cut it."
The young larks huddled together in the nest, very worried.
When their mother returned, they all chirped at once and begged her to move them somewhere safe.
"Did the farmer say he would cut the wheat himself?" she asked.
"No, he will ask his neighbors to help," they answered.
"Then there is no need to worry yet," said the mother lark, and she calmly fed them their supper.
The neighbors were busy harvesting their own fields, so nobody came.
A few days later, the farmer returned and said, "Tomorrow we will ask our cousins to help us."
Once again, the young larks were upset, but their mother stayed calm.
"Cousins have their own work to do," she said. "We can stay here a little longer."
On his third visit, the farmer looked at the ripe wheat and shook his head.
"We cannot wait for anyone else," he told his son. "At sunrise tomorrow, you and I will cut this field ourselves."
When the mother lark heard this, she gathered her young ones at once.
"Now it is time to leave," she said. "When a farmer decides to do the work himself, it will certainly get done."
That evening, the whole family flew to a new home beside the forest.

credit.title: The Lark and Her Young Ones
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Harbor Fun Run
sentences: Every June, Harbor Town holds a five-kilometer fun run along the harbor path.
This year, Leo wanted to finish in under thirty minutes, so he had trained three mornings a week since March.
Maya was entering the race for the first time.
She had never run farther than two kilometers before, and her only goal was to finish without stopping.
Leo started fast and passed many runners in the first kilometer.
By the fourth kilometer, his legs felt heavy, and he had to slow down.
He crossed the finish line, looked up at the big clock and saw thirty-one minutes.
Leo put his hands on his knees and stared at the ground.
He had missed his goal by one minute.
A few minutes later, Ana, who was helping at the finish table, came over with a list of last year's times.
"Look," she said, pointing at his name. "Last year you finished in thirty-four minutes."
Leo read the list twice.
He had run three whole minutes faster than last year.
He stood up straight, and a slow smile spread across his face.
Just then, Maya came around the last corner, running slowly but steadily.
When she crossed the line, she threw both arms in the air and shouted, "I didn't stop once!"
Her time was forty-two minutes, but she did not even glance at the clock.
Leo and Ana cheered for her, and Leo suggested that next year they could all train together.

passages.title: The Day the Sun Went Dark
sentences: Last spring, my family drove for six hours to stand in the path of a total solar eclipse.
During a total eclipse, the Moon passes exactly between Earth and the Sun and covers the Sun completely.
This can only be seen from a narrow strip of land, and any one place may wait hundreds of years between total eclipses.
I had been reading about it for months, and I wanted to see it more than anything.
On the morning of the eclipse, I woke up early and looked out of our motel window.
Thick gray clouds covered the whole sky.
My stomach felt tight, and I could hardly eat any breakfast.
My dad studied the weather map on his phone, and we drove another hour west to a field where the forecast showed clear sky.
By noon, the clouds behind us had thinned, and the sky above the field was bright blue.
I let out a long breath, and my shoulders finally relaxed.
We put on special eclipse glasses, because looking straight at the Sun without them can damage your eyes.
Through the dark lenses, I watched the Moon slowly cover more and more of the Sun.
As the last sliver of sunlight disappeared, the air grew cool, and the birds in the trees went quiet.
The sky turned a deep blue, almost like night, and a few bright stars appeared.
Only during those few minutes, while the Sun was completely covered, was it safe to take our glasses off.
Where the Sun had been, there was a black circle with soft white light streaming out around it.
Everyone in the field cheered, and then they went completely silent.
I stared at it the whole time, and I forgot to take a single photo.
After about three minutes, a bright flash of sunlight burst from one edge, and we quickly put our glasses back on.
On the long drive home, I kept thinking about how tiny our field had looked under that strange, dark sky.
I have already marked the next total eclipse I can travel to on my calendar.

credit.title: The Day the Sun Went Dark
credit.author: Learning to Fly (AI-drafted)

passages.title: The Whale Watch
sentences: Every summer, small boats carry visitors out from the coast to watch humpback whales feed.
Humpbacks can grow as long as a city bus, and like all whales, they must come to the surface to breathe air.
On one trip last July, a girl of about eleven stood at the front of the boat with binoculars around her neck.
She had read three books about whales, and she knew how to spot the tall puff of mist that a whale blows out when it breathes.
For the first hour, the sea was empty.
The boat rocked from side to side, the wind was cold, and several passengers went inside to sit down.
The girl kept scanning the water, but her shoulders slowly drooped.
"Whales are wild animals, so we can never promise to see one," the captain said over the speaker.
The girl sat down on a bench and put her binoculars away.
Then, far off to the left, a puff of mist shot up from the waves.
The girl jumped to her feet and pointed, shouting, "There! A blow!"
The captain steered closer slowly and turned off the engine, so the noise would not disturb the whale.
A dark, shiny back rolled through the water, and then a huge tail rose high into the air and slid under the sea.
The underside of the tail was black and white, with a pattern of spots and scratches.
The captain explained that every humpback has its own tail pattern, so scientists can use photos to tell the whales apart.
The girl had taken a photo of the tail just before it disappeared.
The captain told her that she could send it to scientists who keep a record of every humpback tail they have seen.
On the ride back to shore, she did not seem to notice the cold wind at all.
She looked at her photo again and again, smiling at the spots on the tail.
